title: Whole-Number Right Triangles Up To N
statement:
Given an integer n, count the triples of integers (a, b, c) with 1 ≤ a, b, c ≤ n and a² + b² = c².

The triples are ordered: (3, 4, 5) and (4, 3, 5) are two different triples and both count.

examples.why: (3, 4, 5) and (4, 3, 5). Swapping the two legs gives a second triple.
The smallest hypotenuse that works is 5, which is out of range.

hints: Three nested loops over a, b and c work for n = 250, but one of the loops is not needed.
Once a and b are fixed, c is decided: it must be the square root of a² + b².
Loop over a and b, compute s = a² + b², and check whether s is a perfect square whose root is at most n.

explain.intuition:
Picking a and b already fixes c: it can only be √(a² + b²). So instead of trying every c, compute that square root and check that it is a whole number and not larger than n.

Use an integer square root (or round the floating one and verify by squaring) so floating-point error never makes a non-square look like a square.
steps: Loop a from 1 to n and b from 1 to n.
If c ≤ n and c · c = s, count the triple.
pitfalls: Only counting a < b. The triples are ordered, so both (3, 4, 5) and (4, 3, 5) count.
Forgetting the c ≤ n bound: with n = 4, (3, 4) gives c = 5, which does not count.
Trusting Number.isInteger(Math.sqrt(s)) without thinking about precision. Here the numbers are small, but squaring the rounded root back is the safe habit.

solutions.title: Try every triple
solutions.idea: Three loops over a, b and c, counting the ones that satisfy the equation.

solutions.title: Two loops and a square root
solutions.idea: For each pair (a, b), the only candidate for c is the integer square root of a² + b².

followups: Loop over a and c instead and solve for b. Can you stop the inner loop early?
Count only primitive triples (no common factor). How does Euclid's formula help?
